Executive Order 13848 has been on the books since September 2018, and the Trump administration's renewal of the national emergency under it means OFAC still has the statutory hook to keep sanctioning foreign election interference networks heading into the 2026 midterms. The framework is operational. Whether it's doing much is a different question. The basic architecture: OFAC designates individuals, entities, and support networks assessed to be conducting interference operations against U.S. democratic processes. Designation triggers asset freezes, transaction prohibitions, and secondary sanctions exposure for third parties doing business with the named actors. The deterrence logic is that raising financial and reputational costs changes the cost-benefit calculation for would-be interference actors before they move. That logic has a structural problem when the actors in question are Russian, Chinese, or Iranian intelligence services. These are state actors whose electoral interference operations run through organs that are already, by definition, largely outside dollar-denominated financial exposure. Designating an FSB officer or a PLA Unit 61398 affiliate doesn't freeze assets they hold in sanctionable jurisdictions, because they don't hold meaningful assets in sanctionable jurisdictions. The designation has signalling value. It names the operation, creates a public record, and potentially complicates the designated individual's international travel and banking in third countries that take OFAC lists seriously. But it doesn't disrupt the operation. Where OFAC designations carry actual bite is against the intermediate layer: third-country companies and individuals that provide technical infrastructure, financial services, or logistical support to interference operations and that do maintain real exposure to the international financial system. A Cypriot shell company running money for a Russian influence network, a hosting provider in a Gulf state processing payments for a disinformation farm, a software vendor in Southeast Asia providing tools to an Iranian operation. These actors have bank accounts that can be frozen, correspondent banking relationships that can be severed, and business interests that are genuinely harmed by designation. The sanctions programme's most operationally meaningful enforcement runs through this layer, not through the primary state actors themselves. The 2026 midterm cycle, by most analytical assessments, is shaping up to be a more complex interference environment than 2024 or 2022. The German Marshall Fund's post-2024 lessons work, Check Point's multi-vector cyber threat analysis, and the Center for Democracy and Technology's election security mapping all point in the same direction: AI-enhanced disinformation that lowers the cost and raises the volume of synthetic content production, tighter integration between cyber intrusion operations and influence campaigns (hack-and-leak is not new, but the amplification infrastructure around it has matured), and more sophisticated exploitation of domestic political polarisation as a force multiplier. Foreign actors have gotten better at identifying and widening existing fault lines rather than manufacturing new ones from scratch. That's harder to attribute and harder to counter. Against that backdrop, the OFAC framework's continued operation sits in a complicated institutional context. The Trump administration has simultaneously maintained the EO 13848 emergency declaration and presided over a significant rollback of the broader counter-foreign-interference infrastructure. The State Department paused foreign misinformation countermeasure programs. The Global Engagement Center, which was the primary State Department mechanism for coordinating counter-disinformation work with allied governments, was shut down. INSS has documented withdrawal from counter-foreign-interference operations more broadly. Intelligence community restructuring has affected the analytical capacity that feeds attribution determinations. The result is an architecture where one enforcement tool (OFAC designations) remains active while the analytical, operational, and diplomatic capacity around it has contracted. That's a significant mismatch. A sanctions designation is a downstream action. It requires prior work: detection, attribution, evidence development sufficient to meet OFAC's evidentiary standards, and coordination across agencies. Shrinking the upstream capacity while keeping the downstream enforcement tool doesn't maintain the programme's effectiveness. It means fewer designations, slower designations, or designations that are less precisely targeted because the analytical substrate that supports them is thinner. There's also a coordination gap with allies. Sanctions on interference networks work better when they're coordinated or at minimum aligned with partner country actions, because a designated actor who gets frozen out of the U.S. financial system can often find workarounds through financial systems in countries that haven't designated them. The GEC's dissolution removed one channel through which that kind of diplomatic coordination on information environment threats happened. The Five Eyes intelligence-sharing relationships and existing Treasury-to-Treasury channels still exist, but the policy-level coordination infrastructure around counter-disinformation has narrowed. None of this means the OFAC framework is irrelevant. It isn't. The designations create legal exposure that shapes how interference networks structure their operations. They generate public attribution that supports investigative journalism and academic research tracking these networks. They complicate financial and logistical arrangements for the intermediate-layer enablers who do have sanctionable exposure. And they maintain a legal and institutional record that can be built on.
